title: Cynthia Erivo Plays Glinda in ‘Nigerian Wicked’ Sketch on ‘SNL U.K.’: ‘She Wants a BBL That Defies Gravity’
description:
Cynthia Erivo spoofed “Wicked” during her stint hosting “SNL U.K.,” this time taking on the role of Glinda in “Nigerian Wicked.”

	Alongside Ayoade
body:
Cynthia Erivo spoofed “Wicked” during her stint hosting “SNL U.K.,” this time taking on the role of Glinda in “Nigerian Wicked.”

	Alongside Ayoade Bamgboye as Elphaba, Erivo — sporting a blonde wig and pink velour tracksuit — starred in a lo-fi, melodramatic version of the Oscar-nominated musical in which the two enemies-turned-friends go off to meet the Wizard of LagOz. 

	In “Wicked,” Erivo’s Elphaba and Ariana Grande’s Glinda express their frustration with each other with the song “What Is This Feeling.” But in the Nollywood version, Glinda simply slaps Elphaba across the face. 
	

	“Glinda, you slapped me!” Bamgboye’s Elphaba says, to which Erivo’s Glinda replies: “Yes, because you are very classless.”


	The sketch also reimagines Glinda and Elphaba’s makeover scene, with Elphaba saying: “Glinda, I can’t afford this!” 

	“When we go to the wizard, it will all pay off,” Erivo as Glinda replies. 

	“The wizard?” Bamgboye says. “But I’m a virgin!” The two then almost share a kiss, winking at fans who ship the characters together.

	When they finally make it to the “emerald, white and emerald city,” Erivo’s Glinda says she wants the Wizard to get her a Birkin bag, whereas Bamgboye’s Elphaba wants a “skinny BBL.”

	A voiceover from the wizard himself, played by Hammed Animashaun, then rings out: “She wants a BBL that defies gravity!”

	After finally meeting the Wizard, Glinda and Elphaba realize that he’s broke. “That’s a nolex,” Erivo’s Glinda says of his watch.

	After the disappointment sets in, Erivo’s Glinda asks, “What do we do now?” 
	

	Glinda and Elphaba finally lean in for a kiss before an explosion effect engulfs the screen.

	“Nigerian Wicked: LGBTQ!” Animashaun’s voiceover concludes.

schema.headline: Cynthia Erivo Plays Glinda in ‘Nigerian Wicked’ Sketch on ‘SNL U.K.’: ‘She Wants a BBL That Defies Gravity’

title: Shia LaBeouf Would Trash-Talk ‘Lizzie McGuire’ While Filming ‘Even Stevens,’ Says Christy Carlson Romano: ‘He Wanted to Be the Number One Show’
description: Christy Carlson Romano, who first broke out on the sitcom “Even Stevens,” has revealed that co-star Shia LaBeouf used to trash-talk competing Disne
body:
Christy Carlson Romano, who first broke out on the sitcom “Even Stevens,” has revealed that co-star Shia LaBeouf used to trash-talk competing Disney Channel show “Lizzie McGuire” and that he was “definitely beefing” with the show’s star, Hilary Duff.

	“Hilary had no clue about that. I’m sure she was doing her own thing, but he would always be kind of like trash-talking ‘Lizzie McGuire,’” Romano said on a recent episode of “The Joe Vulpis Podcast.” “I was always like, ‘We don’t know anything about them. Like why are you…’” she recalled, adding that he was “very competitive.”
	

	She continued: “He wanted to be the number one show on the network. He had to be the number one show because I think his life depended on that show doing well… He had a rough upbringing, and I think he needed that show to do well for him.” Earlier in the episode, the actress explained that while the actors didn’t have “beef” with rival actors at Nickelodeon, there was competition within the network to get the best ratings.


	Last month, ahead of the release of her memoir, “Once Upon a Trainwreck: The Fall and Rise of a Child Star,” Romano said that she and LaBeouf were “like oil and water” while guesting on a podcast, despite being just 14 and 12 years old, respectively, at the time.

	Romano explained that their on-set incompatibility stemmed from how they were raised.

	“I was being raised and brought up to be this type A, I mean exactly like Ren Stevens. Like, you know your lines, you hit your marks, you don’t mess up,” she said. “You’re a New York kid, like that comes with a certain echelon… I was trying to go to pre-college Juilliard… everything we were doing, my mom called it cross-training, came with a certain dollar amount of training.”
	

	In comparison, LaBeouf has long been open about his tumultuous childhood and has said that his father was a recovering addict, and at times abusive. “He was a Venice Beach kind of bum kid,” said Romano. “It’s like that kind of vagrant fun, but also very chaotic and very scary lifestyle, and he was very young to be having that.” She likened his upbringing to the lifestyle depicted in the 1995 Larry Clark film “Kids.”

	Romano later starred alongside Duff in the Disney Channel original movie “Cadet Kelly.”

schema.headline: Shia LaBeouf Would Trash-Talk ‘Lizzie McGuire’ While Filming ‘Even Stevens,’ Says Christy Carlson Romano: ‘He Wanted to Be the Number One Show’

title: Cynthia Erivo Imagines Competing on ‘The Great British Bake Off’ in ‘SNL U.K.’ Opening Monologue: ‘I’ve Got a Soggy Bottom and I’m Freaking Stressed!’
description: In her opening “Saturday Night Live U.K.” monologue, Cynthia Erivo admitted that despite being an almost-EGOT – with an Emmy, Grammy and Tony to he
body:
In her opening “Saturday Night Live U.K.” monologue, Cynthia Erivo admitted that despite being an almost-EGOT – with an Emmy, Grammy and Tony to her name – there’s one accolade she’s still hankering after: no, not an Oscar but “the Hollywood handshake.”

	Erivo, who is hosting this weekend’s episode, was referring of course Paul Hollywood, a judge on cooking competition “The Great British Bake Off’s” (known as “The Great British Baking Show” in the U.S.). The Channel 4 show features Hollywood and Nigella Lawson as judges and Noel Fielding and Alison Hammond as host.
	

	“That’s right. I’m a huge ‘Bake Off’ fan,” Erivo revealed. “It’s an absolute dream of mine to be on that show. But there’s just one problem: I can’t cook under time pressure. I can run a marathon in under four hours, but ask me to bake a cake, well, then I’m screwed.”


	Earlier in the monologue Erivo told the audience the thing she’s asked about most is her trademark long nails. “Not quite sure why. To me, they’re normal. I’ve had them since I was 16,” she said. “They’re an extension of my body, an expression of my soul, and surprisingly practical. I haven’t had to use cutlery in years.”

	Later, she referred to the nails again while picturing herself competing in the “Bake Off” tent. “It would be chaos,” she said. “Making cake batter with one nail, chopping my butter with the other. Noel’s telling me I’ve got 30 seconds left, and Alison just keeps laughing. It’s not funny, Hammond. Seriously, what are you laughing at? I’ve got a soggy bottom, and I’m freaking stressed!”
	

	At which point Larry Dean, dressed as Fielding, jumped onto the “SNL” U.K. stage and warned Erivo she had 30 seconds left.

	“For the cake?” she asked, slightly panicked.

	“No,” he replied. “The monologue! You need to get on the show.”

	At which point she ran through the end, saying: “Okay, 30 seconds. Music. We have music. Blossoms. They’re great. And sketches. I’m in them, and adverts. I’m not in them. We’ve got an amazing show for you tonight. Stick around and watch this!”

schema.headline: Cynthia Erivo Imagines Competing on ‘The Great British Bake Off’ in ‘SNL U.K.’ Opening Monologue: ‘I’ve Got a Soggy Bottom and I’m Freaking Stressed!’

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Cold Open Spoofs Andy Burnham on ‘Gogglebox,’ Prince William on ‘The Graham Norton Show,’ ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ and More
description: “SNL U.K.” ran down the week in TV during its cold open, through the lens of Prime Minister Andy Burnham‘s recent appearance on “Celebrity Gogglebo
body:
“SNL U.K.” ran down the week in TV during its cold open, through the lens of Prime Minister Andy Burnham‘s recent appearance on “Celebrity Gogglebox.”

	Burnham, played by George Fouracres, featured on the show with Liverpool Mayor Steven Rotheram (Emma Sidi) to discuss their favorite television moments of the week. “You know what my favorite program is, Andy?” Sidi as Rotheram said. “That ‘Saturday Night Live U.K.’ You know, my dream is that one day they do an impression of me.” 
	

	The “SNL U.K.” players then spoofed some of the biggest British shows right now, including “The Celebrity Traitors.” Celeste Dring appeared as host Claudia Winkleman, saying: “What happens when we take 22 celebrities who are too famous to play the game seriously, or care whether or not they win, and put them in a castle? The answer: not much to be honest.” 


	Prince William‘s surprise appearance on “The Graham Norton Show,” in which he discussed his love for Christopher Nolan movies and “The Celebrity Traitors,” was also mocked. Jack Shep suited up as Norton, saying to Freddie Meredith as William: “Now, can I ask you a cheeky question?”

	“Oh, here we go,” Meredith’s William replied with a monotone laugh. “Come on then, Graham. I’m always a good sport, as you know.”

	Shep’s Graham then went for it, asking: “Is it true that your brother Harry has reached out this week?” 

	“Shut up!” Meredith’s William shouted in response.

	“The Great British Bake Off” was next, starring Larry Dean as “sleep paralysis demon” Noel Fielding and Ayoade Bamgboye as Alison Hammond, “the only person everyone in the country likes.” 
	

	“Gogglebox” was soon interrupted by Burnham “from the future,” played by “Weekend Update” host Paddy Young, who informed Fouracres’ Prime Minister that a cyberattack is coming, and the only way to stop it is to “tell the country to buy an extra can of beans.” 

	“You’ve done it, shagger!” Young’s Burnham concluded. “You’ve changed the future … Hang on, is that Steve Rotheram? I loved it when they did that impression of you on ‘SNL U.K.'”

schema.headline: ‘SNL U.K.’ Cold Open Spoofs Andy Burnham on ‘Gogglebox,’ Prince William on ‘The Graham Norton Show,’ ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ and More

title: ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of ‘Uncomfortable’ Age Gap With Montana Jordan: ‘He Was a Baby!’
description: There may not have been sex scenes in “Young Sheldon,” but star Emily Osment still requested an intimacy coordinator because of her “concern” aroun
body:
There may not have been sex scenes in “Young Sheldon,” but star Emily Osment still requested an intimacy coordinator because of her “concern” around co-star Montana Jordan’s age. 

	In Jessica Radloff’s new book chronicling the making of the series, titled “Young Sheldon: The (Juicier-Than-Meemaw’s-Brisket) Inside Story of the Hit Comedy,” she explains Osment’s discomfort shooting kissing scenes with Jordan because of their age gap. While filming their initial episodes, Jordan, who played George Cooper, was 18 while Osment, who played Mandy McAllister, was 30.
	

	“That made me uncomfortable. He was a baby! A baby with a mullet. So I spoke to Tim Marx, and obviously they were not able to get one that late in the day, but for the next few episodes they had one there, since the relationship between them escalates,” Osment said. “It made everything easier having one there. I think it’s something that’s really important.”


	She added, “I don’t know if Montana even knew if he could ask for that. Like, let’s give him the option, too. Make him comfortable. And he’s such a sweet kid, I think he would just eat his discomfort. But I love those guys, and I’m really happy it got to the point where they were able to do that [for us].”

	Director Alex Reid acknowledged that because they didn’t have sex scenes on the CBS show, they “totally dropped the ball” while filming kissing scenes between Osment and Jordan.

	“I have a photo between takes of them sitting in that car when we shot that, and they’re looking off in other directions. I showed it to Emily and she said, ‘Yeah, that was so uncomfortable for both of us, because we didn’t know each other.’ It wasn’t even about the lack of an intimacy coordinator. It’s just you’re having to make out with somebody you just kind of met. Obviously they worked that out, and they have a great chemistry now, but that was kind of embarrassing.”
	

	Co-creator Steve Molaro noted that Osment had “every right to ask” for an intimacy coordinator and eventually “she was comfortable without one.”

	The fictional couple is now at the center of their own show, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” despite the network’s initial concerns about exploring a relationship with such a significant age gap, another subject Randloff’s book explores.

schema.headline: ‘Young Sheldon’ Star Emily Osment Requested an Intimacy Coordinator Because of ‘Uncomfortable’ Age Gap With Montana Jordan: ‘He Was a Baby!’

title: Happy 20th Birthday, ‘Debut’! A Revealing Look Back at Taylor Swift’s First Album, Via a Previously Unpublished Q&A: ‘I Want to Be Here for the Next 20 Years’
description: Today, Oct. 24, 2026, marks the 20th anniversary of the release of Taylor Swift‘s self-titled debut album. It would take at least a few years befo
body:
Today, Oct. 24, 2026, marks the 20th anniversary of the release of Taylor Swift‘s self-titled debut album. It would take at least a few years before anyone really thought of this as a monumental or transformative event — for country music, and then for pop, and then for pop culture as we knew and continue to know it. Who could have known when she was singing about looking for “A Place in This World” while being on “The Outside” at 16 that she’d go on to become the music world’s ultimate insider and biggest star? A visitor from the future making any such claims in October 2006 would’ve been laughed back into his time machine, as Swift’s team was virtually begging to interest journalists in interviews and strugglig to convince country radio to take a chance on a kid who checked off exactly zero of the right boxes.

	It’s unknown whether Swift is baking a cake or doing anything else to celebrate her baby turning 20. She’s not marking it by doing anything so obvious or fan-servicing as putting out a deluxe version of “Debut” (as it’s come to be informally called, for expedience). She’s leaving the world of Swifties to throw their own party for the record that changed everything, first of all for the star herself, but also in starting the process of dramatically resetting expectations for just how open and confessional pop superstars would forever afterward be asked to be, especially as women took over after the boy-band wave washed back out to sea.

	Speaking of time machines: Let’s take one back to when “Debut” was cresting, albeit still far from the peaks that she would reach with its followups. I interviewed Swift at length for Entertainment Weekly on a couple of occasions between the release of her first album and “Fearless.” The first time was in early 2007 when she was getting her hair and makeup done for the ACMs in Las Vegas. The second and more substantial interview was in January 2008, at an In-N-Out burger joint just outside of Universal City. Hard as it is to believe now, only one person approached her for an autograph during the entire hour-plus that we were sitting there enjoying our double-doubles. The vast majority of her success at that point had been in the country sphere, which was much more walled-off from pop then than it is now. And with L.A. not being country central, that might explain why we were able to talk virtually uninterrupted. But MTV was just then starting to experiment by giving a “pop remix” of “Teardrops on My Guitar” some spins, hoping this Nashville cowgirl would be more of a turn-on than turn-off to the “TRL” crowd. How brave of them, right?

	Only a few hundred words’ worth of excerpts from that In-N-Out interview made it into my coverage at the time. Now, for the 20th anniversary of “Taylor Swift,” I revisited those tapes and am pleased to bring up a largely unabridged Q&A taken from that conversation, for the first time, offering a good deal of insight into her early career and how she was thinking at the time about the songs on “Debut,” now that she was a month or so into being a wisened woman of 18.

	Looking back on my notes, I remember being struck by a culinary peculiarity that might have counted as a dieting tip: Swift didn’t drink he entire shake; she used it as a dipping sauce for her fries. I might have to revisit that Universal City In-N-Out this weekend, sit at the same table and see if she was onto something with that dining formula. Hundreds of millions of U.S. album and singles certifications later, one tends to put some faith in her judgment.

	Swift: [Talking to then-publicist Paula Erickson, who is collecting her order.] I want a No. 2 with no onions and a chocolate shake… [Turning to me.] It doesn’t count if you eat it out of town. That’s a rule.

	Since you’re not from around here, when was your first In-N-Out experience?

	My first In-N-Out Burger experience was probably about a year ago. I became addicted, and it’s a deep love. It runs deep.

	Your publicist, Paula, and I had a disagreement. She said she loves coming here but hates the fries.

	How could she say that? How could she say that? Oh, gosh. No, the fries are amazing. She just needs to open up her mind to fresh French fries. They make everything fresh. How could you not like that?

	You were on the Leno show last night. How was that?

	That was my second time playing Leno. It’s cool, he’ll bring you a present in the dressing room every time. The first time it was a watch; the second time it was this really cool blanket. Jay always comes and says hi, no matter who you are or where your single is on the chart.

	I’ll tell you a secret: I’ve been in the dressing room with artists a number of times, and Jay always stops in, but I have not seen him bring anybody else a gift.

	[Laughs.] They just know how to treat their guests.

	You have two songs charting — “Our Song” is huge at country, and “Teardrops on My Guitar” is just starting to give you some of your first top 40 airplay. Was it tough to decide which to do?

	Whichever one is No. 1. For me, it was kind of a no-brainer to play “Our Song,” because it just got its sixth week at No. 1 on the country charts. And on “Dick Clark’s Rockin’ New Year’s Eve,” I got to play both. But when there’s a choice for me, I usually pick the one that’s higher up on the charts. I’m gonna milk this No. 1 for all it’s worth.

	It’s surprising neither of the two earlier songs went No. 1 at country, in retrospect [“Teardrops on My Guitar” peaked at No. 2].

	I was lucky enough to have the songs impact really well with people. They didn’t ever get to No. 1 chart status, but I felt like they both did something really good for my career. But having my first No. 1 be a song that I wrote by myself in 9th grade for my talent show in high school, that’s kind of surprising. I didn’t even see that one coming. So it’s very exciting to be No. 1 and stay No. 1.




	

					Taylor Swift during 2007 CMT Music Awards – at The Curb Event Center at Belmont University in Nashville, Tennessee, United States. 
									FilmMagic, Inc
	



	There are probably people who are still suspicious because of your age, that you are really writing the songs… but looking at which ones you wrote by yourself, no one can look at “Our Song” and doubt that you’re a songwriter.


	Thank you. I’m actually really thrilled that that’s the song that was my first No. 1, because it kind of says something. I’ve always wanted that respect from the songwriting community in Nashville, and this year I was lucky enough to get the NSAI songwriter artist of the year award, which is voted on strictly by songwriters. And to get my first No. 1 with a song I wrote by myself, it really means a lot to me.
	

	Being older, a lot of times I don’t connect with specificially quote-unquote teenage music…


	No offense taken, it’s OK!
	

	But all that’s to say, though I don’t always have a lot of nostalgia about being that age, there’s something about the sweet specificity of “Our Song” that I can listen and, for three minutes, at least, go, all right, maybe I do wish I was a teenager again.

	Oh, that’s really sweet. Thank you. That was one of those songs that I wrote in 20 minutes, literally just sat down and wrote out the whole thing. You know, I never expect to win if I’m nominated for an award. I never expect to have a song go No. 1 if I put it out. I would never expect a song that I wrote by myself in 9th grade would make the album and then be a single and then be a No. 1.

	You also wrote “The Outside” by yourself.

	I was 12, yeah.

	And there’s a song on your recent Christmas EP you wrote by yourself.

	I wrote “Christmas Must Be Something More” when I was 13. I like to go back and look at the stuff I wrote when I was younger and include it, because there’s a place for that, and there’s a place for the vulnerability and the innocence in the songwriting. I wrote “The Outside” about not fitting in at school—about the scariest feeling I’ve ever felt, which is going to school and walking down the hall and looking at all those faces and not knowing who you’re gonna talk to that day. It’s scary when you’re 12. I mean, it’s scary at any age to go through that. And a lot of people ask me, how did you have the courage to walk up to record labels when you were 12 or 13 and kind of jump right into the music industry? It’s because I knew I could never feel the kind of rejection that I felt in like middle school. I could never feel that in the music industry, because they’re polite. If they’re gonna say no to you, at least they’re gonna be polite about it, at least. … First of all, I didn’t know any better. And second of all, I hadn’t had the most perfect social life in middle school, so I guess it got me ready for the real world, in a sense.

	You mentioned that when I first interviewed you last spring, and at the time I wondered, why did she feel that way? Somebody would look at you and think you were one of the popular kids. But you were clearly precocious — did that separate you from your classmates?

	I think what separated me was that on the weekends, all of the friends that I had were starting to party already — were going to parties, were starting to steal alcohol from their parents. And I just was never into that. I never was even tempted by it. What I was doing on weekends was going to singer/songwriter nights, and playing guitar for people, and sneaking into karaoke bars, and going to festivals and plugging in my guitar into little crackling amplifiers — that’s what I was doing. So I think that naturally separates you, if you’re not doing the same things other people are doing. You know, I wasn’t at soccer practice talking to them, and I wasn’t at the parties hanging out with them. So I think that that obviously was the split between me and them.

	As you did a lot of singing, did you do it in your community, and find that it helped you forge relationships with people, or were you always off on your own doing it more privately?

	I feel like I was a little bit more on my own doing it, because I was from a small town, and nobody really expects you to leave, especially before you graduate. That doesn’t really happen. So it was a very rare case, the fact that I left. And I actually went back a couple months ago and played a sold-out show in my hometown, and it was absolutely amazing. Ever since all this stuff has started happening, the people in Pennsylvaia been the most supportive people I’ve ever known. But I wouldn’t change a thing about growing up and not exactly fitting in. If I had been popular, I wouldn’t have wanted to leave, probably. It would have been harder, at least.

	When did you actually move to Hendersonville from Pennsylvania?

	I got to Hendersonville when I was in 8th grade, and it was the best place that I’d ever been. People all of a sudden didn’t look at me like I was weird because I played music, because that’s what all their dads did. But it’s far enough away from Music Row to where you’re not right on top of all the songwriters; you’re not right on top of all the publishing companies. It’s a 20-minute drive away, but you’re not right there. My family moved to Nashville because I was so obnoxious about wanting to go. When I was 10, and when I was younger than that, even, I would watch these biographies on Faith Hill or the Dixie Chicks or Shania Twain or LeAnn Rimes, and the thing I kept hearing was that they had to go to Nashville, and that’s when they made it big. And so I kept saying to my mom, “Please, I want to go to Nashville — that’s where I need to go, I need to be there.” And eventually she said “OK, we’ll take a trip there, we’ll see what happens. You can take your demo CD” that I recorded of karaoke songs, and I sound like a chipmunk — it’s pretty awesome. She’s like, “You can go and take a trip and knock on doors and see what happens.” So my mom and me and my little brother got on a plane and we went to Nashville when I was 11, and I knocked on doors up and down Music Row. My mom would wait in the car, and I would say, “Hi, I’m Taylor, I’m 11, I want a record deal. Call me.” That sort of thing. And nothing happened, of course. But I went back home with this feeling that I needed to be different, and it just motivated me even more, the fact that it wasn’t easy. That somehow was even more of a motivator to me, and more of a challenge, and I loved it. So that’s when I started playing guitar and writing my own music, and I said, that’s gonna be my thing. That’s what’s gonna make me different. So I spent the next couple years working on my craft and honing in on my skills and practicing guitar until my fingers bled, and writing songs every chance I got. And went back to Nashville, and moved there with my family. I was like, “You guys, I’m so serious about this.” And my parents have always encouraged me to do what I feel is my dream. I’m so blessed that my parents were willing to move across the country for that.
	

	Were there any success indicators prior to the move? Did anyone encourage you so it didn’t seem like quite such a huge leap of faith?

	I had been going to Nashville every couple of months, and I got a development deal with RCA on one of my trips, which… I mean, labels have so many artists under development.

	[A boy steps up to the table: “Miss, can I take a picture with you?” She responds: “Of course. Does your mom have a camera? What’s your name, sweetheart?… He’s really cute…. Where was I?” She resumes.]

	A development deal is kind of like a “we’ll see how it goes” kind of deal — “we’ll develop you for a year” — and then after a year they renegotiate and see if they want to sign you to a regular, real, full-on record deal. So I moved to town because of this development deal. Even though nothing was set in stone, I wanted to go. And because of that, I went in and I met with publishing companies, and I became the youngest person ever signed to Sony/ATV Publishing for my songwriting. I was 14. So my mom would pick me up from school and I would go downtown and write with songwriters all day after school, and then I would go back home and do my homework and do the same thing all over again the next day. I really was trying to get respect as a songwriter, too, and get myself known that way. The year came up with RCA, and they wanted to develop me for another year instead of sign me. I decided to walk and see my other options. And that doesn’t happen, because that’s a huge, awesome record label; they have all the stars on that record label. I just wanted to explore other options, and that’s when I met Scott Borchetta, who was then working at Universal. I thought, oh, awesome, I’m gonna get to deal with Universal! I get this call a couple of weeks later, after I do this showcase and Scott’s on board and rocking. I get this call and he goes, “I have good news and bad news. The good news is I want to sign you, and the bad news is I’m not gonna be with Universal Records any more.” Because he was leaving to start up this whole new record label.

	If I recall correctly from our previous interview, you getting out of the development deal was partly because they wanted you to record outside material.

	I think that probably had a lot to do with the fact that I was 14. And there had been no teenager that had worked out in country music since LeAnn Rimes, and that was 1996 when she came on. So it had been 10 years since any teenager had worked out in this industry, so a lot of people were afraid of that. So it didn’t work out. I’ll always be grateful to them for giving me that first leg up in the music industry. I will never say a bad thing about them. RCA Records and Joe Galante and Renee Bell were unbelievable, that they gave me that chance and signed me when I was 13. It just didn’t end up being the way that my career ended up going. What ended up happening was, I ended up signing with a record deal with a record label that didn’t even have a name or furniture. It had 10 employees, and it was a total leap of faith, but somehow it worked out. We had 10 employees at the record label, so my mom and I all came in, when they were releasing my first single, to stuff the CD singles into envelopes to send to radio. Because there were other people that were just having to do their jobs, and there weren’t enough people. We sat out on the floor and did it because there wasn’t furniture at the label yet.

	So, to make a list of the odds that were stacked against you: (a) Being a woman, for starters, seems to count as a strike with the country radio audience. (b) The teen thing, as you said. (c) You are one of the first artists for a fresh label startup. (d) Using your own material was a bad thing to do, supposedly. It’s a pretty long list! It’s a tough time for new artists in any field of music, but in country, especially, Ashley Monroe and some other promising young female artists have been getting dropped from major labels…

	Love Ashley.

	Do you wonder whether anyone is learning anything from your success, or do they just still need, like, another Taylor Swift to come along to further prove something?
	

	I hope people look at what’s happened with me, growing a fan base on MySpace, writing their own material. I hope that there are other artists like that, honestly. I want country music to be a first-rate music. In a perfect world. I would think no one’s saying “I hate country music.” I want country music to be as good as it can possibly be, and I want there to be a base of artists that bring people from everywhere to this format. And I think that it’s moving in that direction.



	

					Musician Taylor Swift poses during the 50th annual Grammy Award Nominations held at the Henry Fonda Music Box Theatre on December 6, 2007 in Hollywood, California.  
									Getty Images
	



	Something people aren’t even talking about that much with the success at radio is your album making the Soundscan top 10 for the year. I like to pride myself on seeing things coming, but I didn’t foresee that.

	Trust me, I’m more shocked than all of us. The album is back to No. 1 again for the fifth week in a row. It just blows my mind, it really does. The album has been out for so long — over a year — and it’s just now having a top-selling week. [The No. 1 status she was referring to was on the country albums chart; on the overall Billboard 200 chart, it peaked at No. 5, and was her only album to fall short of No. 1.]

	I don’t mean this to sound like a putdown at all, but you’ve achieved all this success and there are still a vast majority of people who haven’t heard of you.

	That’s what is so exciting, and what keeps me going on a daily basis is the fact that I know nothing compared to what I’m gonna know a year from now. I know nothing. We haven’t tapped into half the people we’re gonna tap into, and I haven’t even been exposed to one-tenth of the people I want to be exposed to. The things that we have yet to do really just fuel me and make me so happy.

	[The boy who asked for the autograph earlier returns. She says, “It was good to meet you, Tyler; give me a handshake. Good luck with your movie. You’re welcome.”]
	

	You have success starting to happen at CHR [top 40 radio]. What does that mean to you? Carrie’s song (“Jesus, Take the Wheel”) broke the logjam (of crossover between country and pop), but it’s been a long time since that really happened.

	Yeah, with the crossover stuff, it’s like, I didn’t see that coming either. I write country music and I didn’t see it crossing over. But when the idea was brought up by Universal Republic, I was like, yeah, I’m on board. I don’t look at it as crossover as much as I look at it as spillover. Not as much transferring myself from one place to another, but just there being the offshoot, and it just kind of spilled over into a different category. I’m so lucky that that has happened. I love it when I turn on a pop radio station and hear my song. It makes me so happy. Like we were talking about, those people are just now hearing my name for the first time.

	You just got nominated for best new artist at the Grammys. You were at the announcement ceremony, and you had a big reaction when your name came up. Were you confident that was coming?

	I was being optimistic, but you don’t know. I went in there not knowing. And they read off all the country nominations first, and I didn’t hear my name. And so I just thought, you know, it was cool to come out here — I always like being in L.A.; thank you for inviting me, that sort of thing. So I’m standing back there and not really even listening intently, as they were announcing the nominees for best new artist. And I remember just screaming and hugging everyone on the stage. It was so amazing.
	

	I wonder how many people in Nashville were seeing you on TV for the Grammy nomination and how long it takes them to remember: “Holy crap, that’s that little girl who knocked on my door a few years ago.”

	I’ve heard stories about how everyone’s been passed on in Nashville by somebody, and there’s always somebody who is like, “Oh gosh, I passed on that.” But I think they also know that nothing works without it being the exact circumstances. If one of the circumstances had been different — if I had been at a different label, and they wouldn’t have let me write my own music, and they wouldn’t have let me put music I wanted to put on the album, and they wouldn’t have put out singles that made this album — maybe I wouldn’t be here talking at this In-N-Out Burger fine dining location. It’s all circumstantial. It’s all what happens to add up and make certain things happen in that right order at the exact right time. And a lot of it’s timing. So I think that while people can say, “Wow, she was in my building, wow, she played that song for me that’s now No. 1,” I think everybody kind of knows that without the exact circumstances to produce this, it would have been different.

	Everybody talks about who passed on the Beatles. It would be hard to be in that position, of being one of the A&R people who passed, because every day they meet so many singers who might be just kind of deluded but have the same confident attitude you had.

	Mm-hm. A&R people have the hardest job, because sometimes they’ll believe in something that other people don’t believe in, and they go with their gut and it doesn’t work. And sometimes something that they don’t believe in ends up working. It’s hard to predict that. So I’m never gonna look back on people who didn’t sign me when I was 13 or 14 or 15. I’m not gonna look back on those people and go “Ha — check it out.” Because I wouldn’t be here if they hadn’t passed on me. We wouldn’t be where we are. I think you can be grateful for every single thing that happens. Whether it be a hard experience or rejection or whatever, you have to be grateful for it.

	You are famous for your four-hour autograph sessions after shows. Are you ever at the end of one of those where you think, “Maybe we’re getting to the point where 10 minutes will be just fine”?

	We just did one of those in Nashville the other night. We were literally there four and a half hours. And I feel like in those situations, if those people are willing to stand that long, I am too. And I don’t sit down. If people are willing to wait that long just to meet me, that’s a basic thing, in and of itself. But there are some times when we can’t do it, whether security won’t stay that long or whatever. My manager was talking to me the other day and he’s like, “It’s gonna have to come to a point where you say, I haven’t gotten too big, the crowds have.” But I’m gonna continue to do it as long as I can.
	

	It’s probably safe to say you were always mature for your age, if not already the consummate pro. You were 16 when this process seriously started, but it’s been described as 16 going on 35 in terms of your professional know-how. You’ve been so grown up for so long — but do you ever have moments where you just think, “Oh my God, I can’t handle this, I’m still a kid”?

	I think that no matter what, you’re gonna have those moments, in whatever career path you choose, where you feel like you’re not in control or you feel like it’s all too much, whether you’re getting ready to go to college, which is what I would be doing right now, or you’re picking what you want to do for the rest of your life, or you’re just starting out a new job. You’re gonna feel like you’re not in control. And yes, I have moments like that too. I’m a normal human being. Sometimes I feel like I need to just stop and take a second and not think about it. But then I take my five minutes and then I jump right back into it. Because at the end of the day, I want to be here for the next 20 years, and I can’t do that if I just escape it all and turn it off and pretend like I don’t have to worry about it and hire somebody to take care of it. If I want to be in charge of my own future, I have to be in charge of my career, and I have to be in charge of making decisions I don’t necessarily want to have to make.

	A few years ago I was doing a story on a rising teenage star and, for better or worse, the headline called her “the anti-Britney.” People might think of you that way now, as someone who is appealing to a similar age group as some of the top pop stars but represents something totally opposite in some way, whether that’s music or attitude or lifestyle.

	You know, being compared to Britney… I haven’t been hounded for the last couple years of my life. I haven’t been completely mobbed everywhere I go. I don’t know what that’s like. I imagine I would go crazy if every single thing I did, there were 30 photographers taking pictures of it. So I don’t know what that’s like, so I can’t ever speculate. But I don’t drink, no. I don’t do drugs, I don’t party, I don’t go out, really, at all — I’m kind of boring. I don’t know if that makes me the anti-Britney or just a different kind of person.

	Some of your songs are specifically teenage in their concerns, and some are more universal about love. I think you said you were a freshman when you started to write “Tim McGraw” and you had a boyfriend who was a senior. You said last year you were too career-focused to have a relationship. If you stay single, are you gonna run out of material?

	No, no. You want to hear my new career philosophy and my relationship philosophy? When I find someone who fascinates me as much as my career, I’m gonna go for it. I’m not opposed to dating. I just haven’t found the right person that I’m gonna date. But as far as running out of material: If you’ve been cheated on once, you never forget that feeling. And you never forget what it’s like to have someone break up with you. You never forget what it’s like to have somebody completely act in a way that you don’t understand, and you’re like, “What is going on with you?” If that happens to you once, it doesn’t need to happen again. You know what it’s like. So for me, if I have to go back to when I was 15 and felt something like that, I will. Or, you can write a song about a friendship or a business relationship that sounds so much like a breakup, you can’t even tell the difference. I’ve done stuff like that for my next album. I mean, there’s a song that I wrote with Colbie Caillat that is going on my next album (“Breathe”), and she’s gonna sing harmony on it. The song is not about a relationship or a breakup, but it really, really sounds like it is. And anyone who hears it will think that I wrote it about the most painful breakup of my life, when really I wrote it about losing a friend.

	You don’t mean through death…

	No no no, not through death, thank God.
	

	When you sing songs like “Should Have Said No,” you do it with a lot of, well, vigor.

	I wrote that right after I got cheated on, by the way. Bad cheater guy. Yeah, every lyric in that song is exactly how it happened. I got cheated on by this guy I was kind of dating — you know, when you’re like starting to date someone, and you’re not officially boyfriend-girlfriend yet, but you’re kind of going in that direction…

	Every song feels unusually personal.

	I think the unique thing about me is that I write everything and I don’t edit out names or details or personal details. I’m not afraid to let people in. I don’t have the highest or strongest voice in the music industry. But I write what I feel, and that’s pretty much all I can do.

	A word that describes the approach of a lot of my favorite songwriters is “conversational.”

	Thank you. You know what? That’s what I was trying to put my finger on, and that is how I would explain my singing style. It is very conversational. My singing style is catered to the songs that I write, and a lot of times the songs that I write are very conversational. So you totally hit the nail right on the head there. Say that instead of what I said — that it’s conversational! And pretend that I came up with it. Yeah, conversational. Especially with “Our Song” — totally conversational, probably the most conversational song I’ve ever put out, and it’s done the best of all of them.

	As far as putting people’s names in songs, has anybody objected?
	

	I kind of feel bad for guys a little bit, after I’ve written songs about them with their names in them and stuff, because they move on to different relationships, and their new girlfriends are always like smacking them in the car when the song comes on. But I think songwriting is the ultimate form of being able to make anything that happens to you in your life productive. If you get your heart broken, or if you get out of a bad relationship that was just a complete waste of your time and a waste of your emotions and waste of everything, you can write a song about it and it can become a benefit to your career. How sweet is that?

	But you must’ve had some happy experiences with boys, to get “Tim McGraw” and “Our Song.”

	Of course, of course. I had one cute little relationship.

	All the happy songs came out of one relationship?

	Yeah, “Tim McGraw” and “Our Song” are written about the same guy. And all the rest are written about various people. I think it’s funny, because it kind of sounds like I’ve dated a lot of people, if I could have written that many songs about guys. But you don’t have to date somebody to write a song about him. You don’t even have to know their name to write a song about somebody.

	We were talking about “Teardrops on My Guitar” earlier when my tape recorder shut off. You were talking about Drew coming up the driveway.
	

	As far as Drew coming up my driveway, I was on my way to go to a hockey game, and my dad came up to me out in the driveway and he said “Hey, there’s someone here to see you.” And it was Drew from “Teardrops on My Guitar.” And I was like, “Wow! Hi! You’re late.” I hadn’t talked to him in like three years, so it was kind of interesting seeing him again.

	But you had seen his MySpace page in the meantime, right?

	Yeah, his MySpace about me is “Hi, I’m Drew, and my one claim to fame is that I have a country song written about me.”

	You said some of your songs are so personal, you didn’t have a lot that were cover-able, because you wrote so specifically. But you have written a song with Kellie Pickler that wasn’t for yourself. You enjoying the idea of moonlighting?
	

	Oh yeah, it’s cool to jump into somebody else’s life. Just from stuff that Kellie had told me from being her friend about this ex-boyfriend relationship, I was able to look back to one of my old relationships, where he’s got a new girlfriend and the new girlfriend hates you, and that sort of thing. It’s a hilarious, amazing song that’s going on her next record (“The Best Days of Your Life”), and it feels so good to have one of your babies, one of your songs, going a different place. Possibly, I could have two songs on the chart, if Kellie releases hers and I release one of mine. That would be so cool. It is so hard, though, to give up something, because you never know where it’s gonna go. But being friends with Kellie, I hope that’s a No. 1 song for her.

	You’ve had three songs become country hits off this album, which is a nice streak. I will say I was surprised you passed over “Picture to Burn,” which seems like a really obvious hit.

	That’s coming next.

	So you knew to save the feistier ones for later.

	[She laughs.]

schema.headline: Happy 20th Birthday, ‘Debut’! A Revealing Look Back at Taylor Swift’s First Album, Via a Previously Unpublished Q&A: ‘I Want to Be Here for the Next 20 Years’

title: Billy Corgan Says He’s Stood by Marilyn Manson Despite Sex Abuse Claims Because He ‘Didn’t Feel He Was Guilty’: ‘I Don’t Want the World to Tell Me Who My Friends Are’
description: Billy Corgan remains steadfast in his relationship with close friend and longtime colleague Marilyn Manson, despite a series of sexual misconduct a
body:
Billy Corgan remains steadfast in his relationship with close friend and longtime colleague Marilyn Manson, despite a series of sexual misconduct and domestic violence lawsuits that have been filed against Manson throughout the years. When asked about the friendship on a recent episode of the New York Times’ “Popcast” podcast, the Smashing Pumpkins frontman responded that he “personally didn’t feel that he was guilty” and that he doesn’t appreciate the world telling him “who I should associate with.”
	

	“As a Christian person, you have to stand by your friends, but that doesn’t mean you don’t have an opinion, and that doesn’t mean you’re not critical,” said Corgan. “I personally didn’t feel that he was guilty of the things he was being charged with, and ultimately, the fact that the DA didn’t pursue… the person that I knew and the way it all kind of went down, even though it was an elongated process, was commensurate with the person that I knew.”


	He continued: “I don’t want the world to tell me who my friends are and who I should associate with. That’s politically or socially. In Brian’s case, we have a relationship that goes back close to 30 years.” Corgan noted that Manson’s wife, Lindsay Usich, is the twin sister of Smashing Pumpkins guitarist James Iha’s wife. “So Manson’s basically a part of our family,” he added.

	“Anybody in that situation struggles with the accusations, the seriousness of the accusations. But again, I also knew the inside baseball of the case. I knew certain people who were involved, and so you make those evaluations. If he’s guilty, or anybody in that situation is guilty, they should go to jail. I’m not saying I have any moral supremacy here. I’m saying it’s a case-by-case basis. This kind of witch mob thing bothers me.”
	

	In 2021, actress Evan Rachel Wood alleged that Manson “horrifically abused” her while in a relationship. She gave a statement to Vanity Fair, and a story in the magazine also featured statements from three other women who accused Manson of abuse. Manson was subsequently dropped from his record label, manager and CAA. In 2022, Manson sued Wood for defamation, though in 2024 he dropped the lawsuit and was ordered to pay her legal fees.

	“Game of Thrones” actress Esmé Blanco also accused Manson of sexual abuse and filed a federal lawsuit accusing him of rape and other acts of sexual violence. At the time, she was one of more than a dozen other women who also made allegations against Manson.

	In 2025, the Los Angeles County District Attorney ruled that Manson would not be prosecuted over allegations of sexual assault and domestic violence. Years prior, in 2018, the Los Angeles District Attorney’s office declined to prosecute sexual assault cases leveled against Manson because of the expired statute of limitations.

schema.headline: Billy Corgan Says He’s Stood by Marilyn Manson Despite Sex Abuse Claims Because He ‘Didn’t Feel He Was Guilty’: ‘I Don’t Want the World to Tell Me Who My Friends Are’

title: What Is ‘Fjord’ Really About? A Political Stance That May Be Too Hot to Handle
description: “Fjord,” Cristian Mungiu’s harrowing and pointedly provocative political drama, has now been open for two weeks, and I have a question about it: Wh
body:
“Fjord,” Cristian Mungiu’s harrowing and pointedly provocative political drama, has now been open for two weeks, and I have a question about it: Where’s the debate? Where’s the fervor, the fire, the discussion, the arguments, the noise, the sense that a movie like this one matters? Everyone is talking about “You Can See Everything,” parsing the nuances of deceit and what is reality and should we blame it on Billy Evans? (we should not). And that’s a conversation well worth having. But when I saw “Fjord” at the Cannes Film Festival in May, I thought it was a movie that would unleash 1,000 conversations, including some highly incendiary ones, since it’s a film that cuts to the spiritual-ideological heart of so much of what’s happening today.
	

	Instead…crickets. Oh, I see the occasional comment on social media, and I’ve encountered a few passionate and withering denunciations of “Fjord.” But where are the defenders, as well as the fireworks of disagreement?


	I think the lack of debate goes back to an experience I had at Cannes that I found at once unsettling and revealing. “Fjord” was quite the conversation piece there — and it won the Palme d’Or, which is one reason it was instantly spoken of as an Oscar contender, not just for best international feature but, potentially, for best picture. I expected “Fjord” to set the media ablaze when it opened. But my experience of how people reacted to it in Cannes is that almost everyone seemed to resist saying out loud what the movie is actually about.

	In “Fjord,” Mungiu tells the story of a family — Mihai Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan), who’s Romanian; his wife, Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), who’s Norwegian; and their five children — who have moved from Bucharest to the picturesque Norwegian coastal village that Lisbet is from. The place feels like a tranquil utopia, and for a short while their lives are good. But then, at school, a phys-ed teacher notices that Elia (Vanessa Ceban), the family’s teenage daughter, has a bruise on the back of her shoulder. It’s clear that she has suffered some kind of injury. The question is raised: Was it the result of violence from one of her parents?
	

	The movie doesn’t suggest that it was; the Gheorghius are portrayed as loving and, in their somber evangelical Christian way, rather gentle people. But when the children are questioned, they own up to the fact that their parents have, on occasion, hit them (in the form of a light smack on the butt). Mihai admits to the police that he’s done this, and also that he has, on occasion, slapped their hands (in a way that’s meant to safeguard them — as in, keep your hand away from the stove). The case becomes an investigation into possible child abuse, and in keeping with the ways of the Norwegian system, the children are immediately taken away and placed in foster care. For how long? An indefinite period. The Gheorghius, it would seem, have done nothing more than, on occasion, lightly smack their children on the rear (something I, as a parent, wouldn’t dream of doing — though it’s not like one or two parents in the Western world haven’t done it). But as they head into a court proceeding, the system looks all but designed to find them guilty. In essence, they face the prospect of having their children taken away, and even the threat of imprisonment, because of a spanking.

	At Cannes, I must have had 50 conversations about “Fjord,” and with two exceptions every single person I talked to had the same interpretation of the movie: that it presented “both sides” of the situation, and that it did not take sides. I heard this over and over again. Yet I couldn’t quite believe it. Simply put, that interpretation does not square with the movie I saw. The other thing that was hard to miss in Cannes is that a great many people didn’t care much for “Fjord.” In the two weeks since the movie has opened, however, I’ve spoken to many viewers who have found it powerful. Yet the wrenching drama I experienced onscreen has, for the most part, not been reflected in the critical dialogue about it. Here are a few thoughts on the film, and on the incredibly telling reaction to it.

	Why do so many insist that “Fjord” doesn’t choose sides? There are no saints in “Fjord,” and the situation it depicts is not without its ambiguities. The Gheorghius are a family of parochial Christians who oversee their children with a sternly tender and rather old-school command, not allowing them to use tech devices to connect to the outside world. When Elia forms a close bond with her renegade neighbor and classmate, Moora (Henrikke Lund-Olsen), her father glowers in silent disapproval of what may be a romantic attraction; the film looks askance at his homophobic conservatism. As “Fjord” goes on, the film suggests that the hermetic nature of how this family is raising its kids is destined to create problems down the line. In that sense, it’s critical of the family. But it’s not as if any of these sins “balance out” the drastic actions of the Norwegian government. To put it in melodramatic terms, the film has a clearly delineated villain.
	

	That villain is the nanny-state. “Fjord” wears the meditative cloak of an art film, but at heart it’s a political docudrama in the classic tradition of the New Hollywood. The movie is based on an actual case in Norway that it sticks fairly close to, with elements of other European cases mixed in. It’s a film like “Norma Rae” or “Z” or “Erin Brockovich,” in which the protagonists are up against an oppressive system — but in almost every instance of this kind of movie, going back 55 years, the system in question is a right-wing government or a corporate behemoth in league with right-wing power. In “Fjord,” the force that threatens the Gheorghiu family is Norway’s progressive bureaucracy — the Child Services agency, which is so programmed to err on the side of safety that it errs, in this case, on the side of grave inhumanity.

	No one watches a muckraking liberal political drama thinking that it gives equal weight to both sides. Well, “Fjord” doesn’t either. But it’s hard to escape the feeling that the reason so many people have rationalized away the film’s moral outlook as a case of both-sides-ism is that they don’t want to acknowledge that a movie that comes from inside the progressive art-film universe — Cristian Mingiu considers himself a liberal — could be critical of the progressive consciousness.

	“Fjord” has been called “a MAGA movie.” Is it? It is not in any way, shape or form. I revere “Fjord” and have no truck with MAGA. At the same time, I’m a staunch progressive who cherishes this movie precisely because I think it’s essential that those of us who carry a progressive sense of justice need to be able to look at our own side and see where it goes astray. “Fjord” is overtly critical of a certain progressive mind-set, one that it sees as rigid and blinkered and even authoritarian. The teachers and school officials who first call the Gheorghius on the carpet, and the Child Services officials who swoop in to investigate and prosecute them, have an infuriatingly smug and blasé manner. They’re talking about taking people’s children away, and they sound like they’re discussing tax law. They know that they have the weight of the system behind then, but what they also have is the weight of an ideology, one that has taken the unassailable issue of children’s well-being and placed it on a pedestal of absolutism.
	

	The movie is about something bigger than “the system in Norway.” Just as “Norma Rae” was about something bigger than the exploitation of cotton-mill workers in North Carolina, “Fjord,” while it’s set with pinpoint precision in a particular time and place, uses the specificity of that setting to make a statement about a more widespread ideological belief system. And that state of mind is: The Child Services officials believe they have the right to take the Georghius’ children away. Legally (in Norway), they do, but what that reflects is a belief in a state authority that is all-powerful — an ironic position coming from those who’ve pledged to protect the powerless from the powerful.

	“Fjord” is an outcry against anti-Christian prejudice. But if that’s the only message you take from it… The movie sets up a spiritual battle between the New Europe progressives and the Old Europe Christians. The Norwegian officials are so suspect of the Georghius’ evangelical roots and practices that their attitude is portrayed — quite rightly — as bigotry. “Am I on trial for my beliefs?” asks Mihai from the witness stand. To a certain degree, he is. But only to a degree. More to the point: If that’s the only message you take away from “Fjord” — that the last thing a government that thinks of itself as enlightened should be doing is clamping down on a family of traditional Christians for their beliefs — then you’ve missed the forest for the trees. For that’s a theme you could get from almost any liberal message movie: Don’t be prejudiced. But that’s not the ultimate message of “Fjord.” The ultimate message of “Fjord” is: Beware a system so convinced of its own virtue that it’s willing to destroy what it’s pretending to save.

schema.headline: What Is ‘Fjord’ Really About? A Political Stance That May Be Too Hot to Handle

title: Horror Fans, Rejoice: FilmQuest Breakout ‘The Crawling’ Is the Gutsy Alien Freakout of Your Dreams
description: For writer and director Christian Everhard, “The Crawling” began as a late-night thought experiment. While on vacation with a girlfriend at an isol
body:
For writer and director Christian Everhard, “The Crawling” began as a late-night thought experiment. While on vacation with a girlfriend at an isolated cabin, he woke up in the middle of the night, his mind racing. As a horror fan, he started thinking about the scariest worst-case scenario. Could a dangerous local break into the house? Could an animal scurry in? 

	And then he saw a bright flash of light he couldn’t account for.
	

	“The Crawling” is, indeed, about a married couple, Mike (Will Brittain, “Kong: Skull Island”) and Emma (Katherine Hughes, “Tell Me Lies”), on vacation in a remote house. One night, Mike is woken up not only by bright lights but also an alien being. Adding to his distress is the fact that Emma thinks he dreamed up the encounter. Things escalate from there, with plenty of twists, turns and extraterrestrial madness.


	But what elevates “The Crawling” is not just alien scares and creature effects — although there are plenty of those, courtesy of Onyx Forge’s Steve Wang & Cleve Gunderman. As “Obsession” launched dozens of think pieces about modern dating, consent and control, “The Crawling” conjures plenty of discomfort from the increasingly fraught relationship between Mike and Emma, which might cut close to real life for many in the audience.



	

									Courtesy photo
	



	Everhard’s first bold choice was centering the film on a character that people might not have empathy for, as Mike’s an alpha police officer on suspension for assaulting a suspect. In a conversation I had with the director following the Oct. 23 world premiere of the film at the Provo, Utah, festival FilmQuest, he explained why Mike was the perfect protagonist, flaws and all.
	

	“Once I figured out what was going to happen to this guy, I started to think, ‘Who would be the one that this would shatter the most?’” Everhard said. “I thought about the guy who defines himself by his manliness and masculinity — not only in his personal life, but also in his work. That started to open the door, and the more I explored it, the more I realized there was an opportunity to peel back the layers of not just gender and identity, but I became transfixed with this idea of, ‘What if I started the film with this guy that the audience probably won’t like?’ He’s presenting as an asshole. I was really interested in trying to see if I could take the audience from not liking this guy to starting to understand him and then start to actually care about him once the ending happens.”

	Mike finds the carefully guarded boundaries of his life quickly eroded beyond his control, many of them even before his close encounter. The couple is on this vacation because they’re trying to get pregnant, and Mike feels everyone is putting the blame for the slow process on him. But what does it say about him if he’s not able to perform or get his wife pregnant as an alpha male should? Meanwhile, Emma doesn’t see the strange things at night that he does … Is he losing his mind? Or, given that she’s a therapist, is she dismissing his reality in order to figure out subtext? As things escalate, their relationship gets squeezed tighter and tighter, and some of the movie’s truest horror is how quickly a relationship can unravel — even if you’re convinced the other person is “the one.”



	

									George Reynolds; courtesy photo
	



	The film’s heavy lifting would fall apart without the complex performances from its leads. Brittain has the flashier role, a once-dominant male eventually stripped to his core, ceding any control. Pair that emotional heft with some truly gnarly body horror, and it could be a breakout part for the talented actor. Hughes is doing some fascinating work in a diametrically opposite role, one that initially signals a manic pixie put-upon wife, but quickly blooms into darker corners as her desires and secrets are revealed.

	“The Crawling” seared itself into my brain and, after a good sleep, it wasn’t just the festival fever that sometimes inspires frenzied praise as a screening lets out. With any luck, horror fans will be able to see this on a big screen and wrap their heads around some of the film’s big questions — many of which I couldn’t touch on here, as not to spoil — and also be thrilled by the alien mayhem.
	

	Watch a teaser trailer for “The Crawling” below.




	“The Crawling” is being represented for sales by producer Nick Donadio.

schema.headline: Horror Fans, Rejoice: FilmQuest Breakout ‘The Crawling’ Is the Gutsy Alien Freakout of Your Dreams

title: Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath Roller Coaster Getting Seat Belts, Will Reopen
description:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Goliath Roller Coaster To Reopen With Seat Belts
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          Goliath Roller Coaster To Reopen With Seat Belts
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 24, 2026
                            11:14 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath roller coaster is set to be reopened with new safety features once the ride has been retrofitted ... after a man was violently thrown to his death earlier this month.
      
    
            The theme park announced seat belts would be added to the ride ... as well as other rides with similar restraints ... CEO John Reilly revealed in a statement Friday.
      
    
            Reilly added ... "Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia remains closed pending necessary safety reviews and clearances. Eight additional rides at five other parks are temporarily closed out of an abundance of caution. Our parks remain open, including throughout Halloween weekend, with more than 220 roller coasters operating across our parks."
      

            We reported earlier ... Hassan Kariem died after he became unrestrained during the ride, flew off the coaster and struck the tracks multiple times.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            In the wake of his death ... parks across the country temporarily halted operations on several high-speed coasters with similar lap bar restraints.
      
    
            Kariem's family told us that he was laid to rest earlier this week.
      
    
            The educator was only 42.
      
    
            RIP

title: 'The Challenge' Star Anika Rashaun Dead at 34
description:
'The Challenge' Star
                          Anika Rashaun Dead at 34 From Breast Cancer
body:
'The Challenge' Star
                          Anika Rashaun Dead at 34 From Breast Cancer
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 24, 2026
                            8:59 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Anika Rashaun -- who starred on hit reality shows like "The Challenge" and "The Real World" -- has died from breast cancer ... her friends have revealed.
      
    
            The TV star-turned-dating coach died on Oct. 1 after being diagnosed with cancer last summer.
      
    
            Cyndi Rich wrote on Facebook ... "Anika shined so bright. Being close to that light as one of her closest friends was a true blessing. She is a vibrant soul. I’ll love her and treasure the 16 years of memories forever."
      

            Another friend Tiara Ramos wrote on Substack ... "Anika Rashaun Walker Rehn was part of my life longer than she wasn’t. She was my mirror: the good, the bad, the ugly, the really ugly. She wasn’t just my friend. She was my other half. If you knew me, you knew her."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Tiara also wrote that despite the fact her mother had breast cancer years earlier ... "she was never identified as high-risk or told by her doctors to prioritize mammograms."
      
    
            She added ... "That was one of the many failures she experienced within the medical system during her time battling cancer."
      
    
            Anika -- who previously appeared on "The Real World" 2016-2017 "Bad Blood" season and on "The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions" in 2017 -- was 34.
      
    
            RIP

Influencer Arrested in Colombia
                          Cops Allegedly Find Glocks, Rifle and Drugs: Report
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 24, 2026
                            1:52 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An influencer born in NYC was arrested in Colombia after authorities claim they found a cache of weapons and drugs inside her apartment ... and the scene they described is straight out of "Narcos" or "Breaking Bad."
      
    
            National police officers and a judge had shown up to Wendy Durán's apartment with a warrant to search the place Monday in order to obtain missing rent payments ... the New York Post reported.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Instead ... cops claim they found two 9mm Glocks and a 5.56-caliber Colt rifle with holographic sights and a laser attachment.
      

            In addition to the weapons ... authorities also say they confiscated a money-counting machine, digital scales, $4,844 in cash, and drugs.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Wendy has since been charged with manufacturing, trafficking, and carrying firearms and ammunition ... she's pleaded not guilty.
      
    
            The Attorney General’s Office said ... "Investigations are ongoing to determine the content creator's potential involvement in other criminal acts, as well as the origin and intended destination of the items discovered."
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            Wendy -- who boasts 8,000 followers on Instagram -- says she uses her brand to "create authentic content that captures attention, builds trusts, and drives results."

Kristi Noem
                          Accused of Creating Fake Press Release After Exiting Latest Job
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 24, 2026
                            2:37 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kristi Noem allegedly created a fake press release using doctored State Department letterhead to explain why she was exiting her special envoy role after getting fired as DHS secretary ... this according to reports.
      
    
            After the State Department announced her exit, Noem shared a press release on State Department letterhead, saying ... "The Special Envoy to the Shield of the Americas role was always a six-month appointment. Secretary Noem remains at the State Department as a Senior Advisor."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            The issue? Sources at the State Department say it was not an official release ... and that the letterhead was fabricated.
      

            A person familiar with the situation told Politico ... "This was not a press release put out by the State Department. Noem went rogue and created a fake letterhead to post on X."
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            An official confirmed the same to CBS News' Olivia Gazis ... who wrote ... "A State Department official confirmed that a statement posted by Kristi Noem to her official envoy account and personal X account was created using fabricated State Department letterhead and was not an official department press release."
      
    
                    
                          
                                  
      
        
    
            We've reached out to the State Department and Kristi for comment ... so far, no word back.
